lessons.title: Welcoming words and a composed posture
lessons.reading: むかえることばとしせいをそろえる

objectives.text: Choose greetings for the person and situation
Demonstrate the standing posture and three bows
Tell colleagues when leaving work or starting a break

sections.title: Voice, expression and attention
sections.body: A greeting is the first step in welcoming a guest who is present. Do more than say the words: face the guest, soften your expression and speak clearly enough to be heard. If you look away and speak quietly, the person may not know whom you are greeting. Show that you are paying attention; this is different from speaking unnecessarily loudly. A pleasant greeting affects both the guest’s stay and the mood of the people working together.

sections.title: Words from arrival to departure
sections.body: The basic welcome is “いらっしゃいませ”; thank departing guests with “ありがとうございました”. Once you have confirmed that you can fulfil a request, acknowledge it with “かしこまりました”. Use “恐れ入りますが” to introduce a request for the guest’s cooperation. Before leaving to check something, say “少々お待ちください”; on returning, say “お待たせいたしました”. The wording changes before and after the wait. When approaching or leaving a guest’s room or dining table, announce yourself with “失礼いたします”. If you cause inconvenience or receive a complaint, apologise and report the matter to the person in charge. Even short standard phrases should be learned together with their situations and actions.

sections.title: Communicating with colleagues
sections.body: Workplace greetings also tell colleagues when your work status changes. Say “おはようございます” when arriving and meeting colleagues, and “お先に失礼します” when leaving before them. Respond to a departing colleague with “お疲れさまでした”. Rather than leaving your station silently for a break, say “休憩に入ります”. Address colleagues by their family name followed by “さん”. Think about whom you are addressing so that you do not confuse guest greetings with internal workplace expressions.

sections.title: Checking your standing posture
sections.body: Straighten your back and draw your abdomen and chin in slightly. Relax your shoulders rather than holding them stiffly. When folding your hands, hold them a little below the abdomen, with the right hand underneath. The material also shows an option for male employees to let their arms hang naturally at their sides. Aim for a natural, calm expression instead of a forced smile. Check from the front and the side: is your back rounded or your chin raised?

sections.title: Choosing a bow for the situation
sections.body: A bow expresses respect through posture. Look towards the guest and say what you need to say before bowing. A light bow, 会釈, involves leaning the upper body forward by about 15 degrees and is used when passing guests or leaving a dining table. 普通礼・敬礼, about 30 degrees, is used in many situations, including welcoming guests. 最敬礼 is deeper, about 45 degrees, and is used when seeing guests off or apologising. Do not memorise the angles alone; practise them with the situation and the respect you want to express.

terms.meaning: A light bow used when passing someone and in similar situations.
A standard bow used for welcoming guests and similar situations.
A deep bow used for farewells, apologies and similar situations.
The area along the centre of the back.
Finishing the day’s work and leaving.

example.situation: You welcome a guest at a ryokan entrance, and a colleague then finishes their shift.
steps: Face the arriving guest and offer a welcome.
Use the standard bow appropriate for welcoming the guest.
Acknowledge the departing colleague’s work with the appropriate expression.

practice.prompt: Check the three bows from the side and act out welcoming, passing and apologising.
expectedPoints: Distinguish approximately 15, 30 and 45 degrees
Speak before bowing
Use different expressions for guests and colleagues

questions.prompt: You return after checking something and have kept a guest waiting. What should you say first?
choices: I’m starting my break.
I’m leaving for the day.
Thank you for waiting.
Please wait a moment.
questions.explanation: On returning, acknowledge the wait that has already happened. This is different from asking the guest to start waiting or greeting a colleague.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate angle of the standard bow, 普通礼・敬礼, used to welcome guests?
choices: About 30 degrees
About 5 degrees
About 15 degrees
About 45 degrees
questions.explanation: The standard bow is about 30 degrees. The light bow is about 15 degrees and the deep bow about 45 degrees. Connect the angle with its purpose.

questions.prompt: Which check of basic standing posture is appropriate?
choices: Raise your shoulders firmly and lift your chin.
Round your back and clasp your hands at chest level.
Turn your back to the guest and only say a greeting.
Straighten your back, draw your chin in slightly and relax your shoulders.
questions.explanation: Adjust your back, chin and shoulders, and face the guest with a natural expression. Stiffness and failure to pay attention to the guest are inappropriate.

questions.prompt: Which pair of messages to colleagues is appropriate?
choices: Leaving first: welcome / Starting a break: thank you
Leaving first: I’m leaving for the day / Starting a break: I’m starting my break
Arriving: thank you for waiting / To a departing colleague: excuse me, but…
Addressing a colleague: family name without さん / Arriving: excuse me
questions.explanation: Distinguish arrival, departure and breaks, and use さん after colleagues’ family names. Do not mechanically reuse guest expressions.

illustration.caption: Angles and situations for light, standard and deep bows
illustration.alt: Compare upper-body forward leans of approximately 15, 30 and 45 degrees against an upright reference.

lessons.title: Using honorific language and considering requests
lessons.reading: けいごでいらいをうけできることをかんがえる

objectives.text: Distinguish respectful, humble and polite language
Listen to unexpected requests and consult a supervisor when unable to decide

sections.title: Making your message easy to receive
sections.body: When giving directions, face the guest and speak brightly and clearly. A smile does not make an inaudible explanation useful. Conversely, a loud voice is insufficient if you do not answer the guest’s question. Check both what you are saying and how you are saying it. In practice, one person explains the facilities while another plays the guest and repeats what they heard. This is an original practice activity, not a fixed procedure taken from the source.

sections.title: Consider possibilities before answering immediately
sections.body: An unexpected request may surprise you, but refusing immediately can rule out workable options. First listen, clarify what the guest wants and consider how it might be provided. However, do not promise something before knowing whether it is possible. Consult your supervisor if you cannot decide yourself. For example, if a guest unexpectedly wants to use a service at a different time, acknowledge the request, explain that you will check and consult the relevant person. “Do not refuse immediately” does not mean “always agree”.

sections.title: Remember the roles of three kinds of honorific language
sections.body: Respectful language honours the actions of the guest or other person. In “お客様がいらっしゃいます”, the person arriving is the guest. Humble language presents your side’s actions modestly to show respect to the other person. In “係の者が伺います”, the person visiting is a member of your own organisation. Polite language uses forms such as “です”, “ます” and “ございます” to address the listener politely. The material also introduces expressions with “お” and “ご”, but this is not an exercise in adding them mechanically to every noun. First identifying whose action you are describing makes it easier to choose the wording.

terms.meaning: Language that honours the other person’s actions and similar matters.
Language that describes your side’s actions modestly to show respect.
Language that addresses the listener politely.
Something the other person wants to have provided or done.
Seeking another person’s advice on a decision or response.

example.situation: A guest asks to use a service later than the time already explained.
steps: Ask what the guest wants and at what time.
Do not agree before knowing whether the request is possible.
Explain politely that you will check, then consult your supervisor.

practice.prompt: Practise receiving an unexpected request from a guest role. How do you distinguish agreeing, checking and consulting?
expectedPoints: Listen to the request first
Consider ways to respond
Consult a supervisor about matters you cannot decide
Distinguish language for the other person from language for your side

questions.prompt: You cannot decide whether an unexpected request can be fulfilled. What should you do?
choices: Refuse without asking why.
Promise that it can definitely be done.
Listen, check and consult a supervisor.
Pretend not to have heard.
questions.explanation: Acknowledge the request and consider ways to fulfil it. If you cannot decide, consult someone rather than making an unverified promise or refusing immediately.

questions.prompt: In “係の者が伺います”, whose action does “伺う” describe?
choices: A staff member on your organisation’s side
The guest
An operation on a booking website
The operation of equipment in the building
questions.explanation: The employee on your side is visiting, expressed with humble language. This differs from respectful language describing the guest’s action.

questions.prompt: Which way of explaining the facilities is appropriate?
choices: A smile is enough, even if the voice cannot be heard.
Recite the explanation quickly without looking at the listener.
Speak loudly and ignore the guest’s questions.
Face the guest, smile and explain clearly.
questions.explanation: Pay attention to the listener and make the explanation easy to hear. Meeting only one element, such as expression, gaze or voice, is not enough.

illustration.caption: Choose wording according to whether the guest or employee acts
illustration.alt: Show a guest’s movement beside an employee’s guidance to compare the roles of the expressions.

lessons.title: Guiding guests and handing over items
lessons.reading: かんないあんないともののうけわたし

objectives.text: Choose how to approach, guide and pass guests
Handle luggage, maps and room keys carefully
Give guests priority in the lift

sections.title: Notice when someone may need help
sections.body: Service does not begin only when someone calls you. If a guest stops in front of a sign and looks around, politely ask what they are looking for. If someone calls you over, respond and give them your attention. Omotenashi means considering how the guest wants to spend their stay and offering thoughtful service. Rather than concentrating only on your own task, observe the guest in front of you and choose your actions accordingly.

sections.title: Where to walk and how to pass guests
sections.body: When guiding someone through the building, a reference position is two or three steps ahead and to the guest’s left. Do not rush ahead: match the guest’s walking pace. If you keep moving faster and the gap grows, you are not guiding effectively. When passing a guest in a corridor, stop briefly, make a light bow and wait for the guest to pass in front. Walking as a guide and passing someone require different actions, so practise them separately even in the same corridor.

sections.title: Luggage and the hand used for directions
sections.body: Handle luggage entrusted to you carefully and carry it inside the guest’s room. Merely leaving it on the correct floor does not finish the task. When indicating a place on a map, face your palm upwards and keep four fingers together. Turn the room key so that it faces the guest correctly, then hand it over with both hands. The orientation easiest for the employee to read may not be easiest for the recipient. Try standing in the recipient’s position to check.

sections.title: Guests have priority in shared circulation areas
sections.body: Even when you need to use the building’s lift for work, give guests priority. Do not enter first simply to finish your task more quickly. Corridors, lifts and room entrances are different places, but the shared question is whether the guest can move comfortably. Add passing another guest and using the lift to a guiding exercise, and practise changing position and movement to suit the situation.

terms.meaning: The speed and rhythm of someone’s steps.
A position slightly ahead and on the left.
Bags and other items carried by a guest.
Both the right and left hand.
Treating something before other matters.

example.situation: You guide a guest who looks lost in the lobby to their room floor and deliver a bag entrusted to you.
steps: Ask which place the guest is looking for.
Walk about two or three steps ahead on the left, matching their pace.
Stop and bow lightly if passing another guest.
Give guests priority in the lift and carry the luggage carefully inside the room.

practice.prompt: Practise guiding in pairs. Include a map and room key and check your actions from the recipient’s position.
expectedPoints: Guiding position and walking pace
A light bow when passing a guest
Hand position when indicating the map
The key’s orientation from the guest’s viewpoint
Guest priority in circulation areas

questions.prompt: You are guiding a guest who walks slowly. What is appropriate?
choices: Stay about two or three steps ahead on the left, matching their pace.
Always walk quickly at least ten steps ahead.
Keep your own speed unchanged to maintain distance.
Go to the destination first without looking back.
questions.explanation: The left-front position and two or three steps are reference points; matching the guest’s pace matters. Letting the gap grow is not effective guidance.

questions.prompt: Which way of handing over a room key is appropriate?
choices: Make it readable to yourself and toss it with one hand.
Put it silently at the edge of the counter.
Turn it to face the guest and use both hands.
Prioritise speed rather than orientation.
questions.explanation: Face the key correctly towards the recipient and use both hands. When using a map, also pay attention to the shape of your hand so the guest can follow.

questions.prompt: A guest is looking around inside the building. What should you do?
choices: Avoid eye contact until called.
Ask whether they are looking for an item or place.
Choose a destination for them and start walking.
Tell them they are interrupting your work.
questions.explanation: Observe the guest and ask what they need. Do not decide their destination without knowing their wishes or ignore signs that they may need help.

questions.prompt: A guest is using the same lift while you are working. What is appropriate?
choices: Employees go first because they are working.
Always make guests wait if carrying luggage.
Decide the order only by work speed.
Give the guest priority.
questions.explanation: Even when work requires use of the lift, guests have priority. Do not prioritise only your own efficiency.

illustration.caption: The guide’s position and pace relative to the guest
illustration.alt: A plan view places the employee two or three steps ahead and to the guest’s left, moving in the same direction.

lessons.title: Considering help that suits the individual
lessons.reading: あいてにあわせたてつだいをかんがえる

objectives.text: Talk at eye level with wheelchair users
Ask guests with visual impairments what help they want
Offer seating according to the wishes of guests who find walking difficult

sections.title: Talk at the other person’s eye level
sections.body: When speaking with a wheelchair user, adjust your position so that your eye levels match. Rather than giving a one-sided explanation from above, consider where it is easy for the guest to talk. The purpose of service is not to finish a fixed movement quickly, but to communicate the information the guest needs. In the original exercise, compare explaining while standing with explaining at the guest’s eye level, then discuss with the guest role which is easier for conversation.

sections.title: Ask what assistance is needed
sections.body: When a guest with a visual impairment arrives, ask aloud whether there is anything you can help with. Do not assume that the guest can see what is happening and move silently; direct your voice towards them. Also avoid deciding their destination before hearing what they want. Today’s practice is a conversation to establish what assistance is needed. Do not regard this short service lesson as sufficient training in specific physical assistance techniques.

sections.title: Connect wishes with ease of movement
sections.body: If a guest using a cane or otherwise finding walking difficult arrives at the restaurant, ask whether they would like a seat near the entrance. Guide them there if that is their wish. Do not assume that a nearby seat satisfies everyone; the guest’s own preference is a condition for this choice. Eye level, assistance needs and seating position are different considerations, but all begin with attending to the individual and checking what they need. In practice, let the same guest role change their preferred seat to check whether the employee is acting on assumptions.

terms.meaning: A chair with wheels used for mobility.
The ability to see with the eyes.
A device supporting the body while walking.
A place for entering or leaving a building or room.
Something the individual wants.

example.situation: A guest using a cane arrives in the dining area.
steps: Ask which seat or guidance the guest would prefer.
If they want a seat near the entrance, guide them there.
Do not decide the seat before checking their wishes.

practice.prompt: Take turns playing guests using a wheelchair or cane and a guest with a visual impairment. Consider what to ask.
expectedPoints: Match the eye level of a wheelchair user
Ask a guest with a visual impairment what help is wanted
Check wishes before guiding someone to a seat

questions.prompt: What consideration does the material indicate when talking to a wheelchair user?
choices: Speak very loudly from a distance.
Match the guest’s eye level.
Decide without speaking to the guest.
Give directions only with a finger, without conversation.
questions.explanation: Choose a position at the guest’s eye level that makes conversation easier. This is not replaced by a loud voice or silent instructions.

questions.prompt: A guest with a visual impairment arrives. What is an appropriate first action?
choices: Silently point at a sign for them to follow.
Decide their destination without asking.
Wait without speaking.
Ask whether there is anything you can help with.
questions.explanation: Speak to the guest and establish the assistance needed. Do not rely only on visual information or decide without knowing their wishes.

questions.prompt: Which seating response is appropriate for a guest using a cane?
choices: Ask whether they prefer a seat near the entrance and guide them there if they do.
Always require them to sit near the entrance without asking.
Always take them to the furthest seat even when they request otherwise.
Do not ask about seating.
questions.explanation: The source makes the guest’s wish a condition. Combine consideration for ease of walking with checking the individual’s preference.

illustration.caption: Match eye level and ask about preferences before guiding
illustration.alt: Show an employee talking at a wheelchair user’s eye level, an offer of assistance and seating near an entrance.

lessons.title: Transferring calls and responding initially to complaints
lessons.reading: でんわのとりつぎとくじょうのしょきたいおう

objectives.text: Prepare to answer calls and transfer them appropriately
Connect an apology and situation check to reporting a complaint
Do not handle everything alone, even when the mistake is yours

sections.title: Preparation and identification when answering
sections.body: On the telephone you cannot see the other person’s expression or gestures. Prepare note paper and writing tools beforehand so you can record necessary details while speaking. When answering, first identify yourself, for example by naming the facility, so the caller knows where they have reached. An original practice opening is “お電話ありがとうございます。青葉旅館でございます” (Thank you for calling. This is Aoba Ryokan), followed by asking the purpose of the call. Check the real facility name and required opening at your workplace.

sections.title: Identify the caller before transferring
sections.body: Before transferring a call to another employee, check the caller’s name and, for a business call, the company name. If you transfer without knowing who is calling, the receiving employee will need to ask again. At the end of a guest’s call, confirm that the guest has disconnected before replacing your handset. Do not end the call the moment you have finished speaking.

sections.title: Apologise, establish the cause and report
sections.body: When receiving a complaint, first apologise for the discomfort caused. Then carefully establish what happened and report it to the person in charge. For example, in an original scenario about missing room supplies, do not interrupt with excuses. Acknowledge the inconvenience and ask about the situation. Practise telling the person in charge both what you heard and what you have already done. Complaints can arise even with thoughtful service, so initial responses need preparation.

sections.title: Do not keep the problem to yourself
sections.body: Even when the cause is clearly your mistake, do not try to resolve everything alone. Keeping it to yourself can delay the response and increase the guest’s dissatisfaction. Apologise, establish the situation and report it to the person in charge. Reporting is not abandoning the guest; it enables an appropriate organisational response. The exercise is about communicating facts, not promising compensation that has not been decided.

terms.meaning: Connecting a telephone call or message to the intended person.
Tools used to write notes.
The part of a telephone used to listen and speak.
An expression of dissatisfaction or a difficulty.
The person responsible for decisions and responses in that work.

example.situation: A guest calls about missing room supplies and you realise that you forgot to prepare them.
steps: Apologise for the inconvenience.
Ask which items are missing and establish the situation.
Report to the person in charge even though you know it was your mistake.
Disconnect only after confirming that the guest has ended the call.

practice.prompt: In groups of three, play the guest, call handler and person in charge to practise receiving and reporting a complaint.
expectedPoints: Prepare notes and identify yourself
Identify the caller before transferring
Apologise, check and report
Do not keep the problem to yourself
Follow the correct call-ending order

questions.prompt: What should you confirm before transferring a call?
choices: The colour of the caller’s clothes
The employee’s lunch
The caller’s name and company name if calling from a company
The purchase price of the telephone
questions.explanation: Check the caller’s name or company so you can tell the receiving employee who is calling. Prepare note-taking tools before answering and identify yourself when you answer.

questions.prompt: What is the basic initial response to a guest’s complaint?
choices: Apologise for the discomfort, establish the cause and report to the person in charge
Immediately argue without listening
Only say it is not your responsibility, then hang up
Treat it as resolved without asking about the cause
questions.explanation: Apologise, check the cause carefully and report. Arguing, abandoning the issue or marking it complete without checking does not address the problem.

questions.prompt: The complaint was clearly caused by your own mistake. What should you do?
choices: Do not report because it was your mistake.
Wait for the guest to forget.
Do not record anything if the person in charge is busy.
Report to the person in charge rather than handling it all alone.
questions.explanation: Trying to resolve everything alone can increase dissatisfaction. Your own mistake is not a reason to omit the report.

illustration.caption: Listen to the guest and pass the details to the person in charge
illustration.alt: Show an employee taking telephone notes, receiving a complaint and reporting to the person in charge.

lessons.title: Serving diverse guests and making supervisory decisions
lessons.reading: たようなきゃくへのたいおうとせきにんしゃのはんだん

objectives.text: Apply the additional Level 2 considerations in practical situations
Check circumstances and outcomes before deciding how to handle complaints
Guide employees and share improvements within the department

sections.title: Include the feet in posture checks
sections.body: When checking the basic standing posture, the Level 2 material also shows heels together and toes slightly apart. Check foot position together with the back and hands. This addition does not make the service posture completely different from Level 1. Treat it as an additional observation point on the same foundation. When coaching an employee, practise identifying the specific part to adjust.

sections.title: Mobility, visual and hearing considerations
sections.body: Barrier-free service helps everyone stay comfortably. In addition to matching a wheelchair user’s eye level, Level 2 describes showing them a wide parking space close to the facility. Approach guests with visual impairments from the front when speaking. For guests with hearing impairments, sign language or written communication may also be used. These categories are not a basis for assuming each person’s condition; they help you consider suitable communication and mobility arrangements. Practise coordinating with a colleague who can provide assistance you cannot provide yourself.

sections.title: Do not omit checks when a key is left inside
sections.body: For a guest who has left their key inside the room, learn the Level 2 sequence of checking the room number and name, accompanying the guest to the room and unlocking it. Do not skip checks and immediately open the room they name merely because they are in difficulty. The material’s checks are the starting point of this lesson. In practice, also follow the facility’s rules for identity verification, authority and unlocking procedures. Do not treat this single statement as a complete set of sufficient identity checks.

sections.title: Coaching for needs and cultural considerations
sections.body: Supervisors guide employees to keep guests’ needs in mind. Rather than simply saying “do it as usual”, consider together where to ask about preferences and what might be adjusted. Facilities welcoming people from different countries and regions should understand and consider cultural and religious differences. Do not practise inferring an individual’s wishes solely from nationality. An original task is to ask the guest about meal or stay preferences and pass relevant information to the responsible employee.

sections.title: Investigate as the person in charge
sections.body: If you are the person in charge, do more than receive reports: investigate where the problem lies and choose a response. For night-time noise, investigate the cause before judging. For a dispute between guests, listen calmly to both sides. If a wallet or other valuable is lost, ask what happened and search as far as possible. Contact the police if theft or another criminal incident is suspected. A serious injury, meanwhile, requires prompt arrangement of an ambulance. Do not group every event into an identical complaint response; different circumstances require different actions and contacts.

sections.title: Confirm outcomes and share improvements
sections.body: Share negative feedback about a stay within the department and consider improvements. If only one individual knows about an issue, it may recur on another shift. When receiving an employee’s work report, the material identifies the outcome as the first item to check. Establish what happened, investigate the cause on that basis and make a decision. Asking about the outcome first does not mean ignoring the sequence of events. In the original reporting exercise, distinguish the outcome, confirmed facts and matters not yet established.

terms.meaning: Communicating by writing.
Opening a lock.
An employee working under someone’s guidance or management.
Signs suggesting a crime or similar incident.
A method for improving a problem.
How an action or event finally turned out.

example.situation: A supervisor receives a report about a night-time noise complaint and feedback about the stay the next morning.
steps: First confirm the outcome of the response.
Investigate the cause of the noise and what was done.
Share the feedback within the department and consider improvements.
Review with employees how they considered the guest’s needs.

practice.prompt: Prepare reports about noise, a lost item and a serious injury. Explain as a supervisor how the responses differ.
expectedPoints: Check the outcome first
Investigate the cause of noise
For a lost item, ask what happened and search; contact police if a crime is suspected
Arrange an ambulance promptly for a serious injury
Share within the department and improve

questions.prompt: Which pair of considerations matches the Level 2 material?
choices: Visual impairment: guide silently from behind / Hearing impairment: speech only
Wheelchair user: distant, narrow parking / Posture: heels far apart
Visual impairment: speak from the front / Hearing impairment: use writing as well
Wheelchair user: avoid matching eye level / Preferences: decide without asking
questions.explanation: Choose methods the guest can receive, such as speaking from the front or writing. For wheelchair users, also learn to show wide parking close to the facility. The added posture point is heels together and toes slightly apart.

questions.prompt: A guest says they left the key inside their room. Which response is appropriate?
choices: Check the room number and name, follow facility identity rules, and accompany the guest to unlock the door.
Open the named room immediately without asking their name.
Give the key to another guest to open it.
Treat a loudly stated room number as complete verification.
questions.explanation: The material describes checking the room number and name, accompanying the guest and unlocking. In practice, also follow facility identity and unlocking procedures; do not omit checks based only on a claim.

questions.prompt: Two guests are in a dispute. What should the supervisor do?
choices: Believe only the person who spoke first.
Always use the same response without investigating.
Leave it entirely to an employee and never ask the outcome.
Listen calmly to both, investigate the circumstances and decide.
questions.explanation: Supervisors investigate where the problem lies before responding. Noise, lost property and injuries also require actions and contacts suited to the circumstances.

questions.prompt: According to the material, what should you check first in an employee’s report?
choices: The reporter’s nationality
The outcome of the response
The uniform colour
The booking website ranking
questions.explanation: First check the outcome, then investigate the cause and decide on that basis. Share guest feedback to improve, and coach consideration of needs, culture and religion.

questions.prompt: Which combination of responses is appropriate?
choices: Serious injury: wait until tomorrow’s meeting / Suspected theft: contact nobody
Noise: decide without investigating / Lost item: do not ask what happened
Serious injury: arrange an ambulance promptly / Lost item: ask, search and contact police if a crime is suspected
Guest dispute: listen to one side / Negative feedback: conceal it within the department
questions.explanation: Serious injuries require an urgent response. For lost items, establish the circumstances and search; contact police if a crime is suspected. Distinguish noise investigation, listening to both sides and sharing for improvement as well.

illustration.caption: Confirm the outcome, investigate, respond and share
illustration.alt: Show a supervisor receiving a report, checking noise, lost-property and guest-dispute situations, and sharing improvements with the team.
